# Syracuse, NY to Rochester, NY Passenger Rail Corridor Proposal

> **Illustrative estimates: costs, schedules and funding figures in this draft come from an uncalibrated planning model and approximate program parameters. They are not budgets or engineering estimates.**

## Executive Summary

This proposal outlines three conceptual alternatives for passenger rail service between Syracuse, NY and Rochester, NY. The evaluated concepts include Alternative 1 (the Existing corridor upgrade), Alternative 2 (the New direct alignment), and Alternative 3 (Via intermediate cities). The evaluation reflects simulated outcomes across 5000 runs per alternative, examining physical footprint, population proximity, delivery schedules, and estimated capital investments.

Capital requirements and timelines reflect tradeoffs among right-of-way approaches. Alternative 1 focuses on existing right-of-way reuse, Alternative 2 applies a greenfield direct alignment approach, and Alternative 3 routes via intermediate points within a 25% detour. Across all three concepts, the station footprint includes Syracuse and Rochester, accounting for 2 stations and 644 thousand residents near stations. Population counts represent proximity within 10 miles of the line and 10 km of stations, which do not represent ridership forecasts.

## Corridor Description

The Syracuse, NY to Rochester, NY corridor encompasses three distinct alignment options. Alternative 1, the Existing corridor upgrade, spans 77 miles with 99.2% of its path on existing rail corridors and 1 miles of new track. It traverses 1 river crossings, 8 environmental flag entries, and 0 miles of new track in flagged areas, with 1.25 million residents near the alignment. Existing rail corridor use does not establish track capacity, ownership access, or operating permissions.

Alternative 2, the New direct alignment, also spans 77 miles but utilizes a 28.3% share on existing rail corridors, requiring 55 miles of new track. Its path includes 1 river crossings, 3 environmental flag entries, 2 miles of new track in flagged areas, and 1.17 million residents near the alignment. Alternative 3, Via intermediate cities, extends 82 miles with a 73.0% share on existing rail corridors and 22 miles of new track. It registers 2 river crossings, 4 environmental flag entries, 2 miles of new track in flagged areas, and 1.28 million residents near the alignment.

## Cost and Schedule Range

Reported capital figures are illustrative estimates rather than final construction budgets. For Alternative 1, the capital cost is estimated at a low (P10) of $1.6B, a median (P50) of $2.0B, and a high (P90) of $2.4B, with a delivery timeline of 8.7 years at P10, 10.0 years at median (P50), and 11.4 years at P90.

Alternative 2 involves an illustrative capital cost estimated at $3.2B at P10, $3.8B at median (P50), and $4.5B at P90, alongside a projected time to opening of 10.6 years at P10, 12.0 years at median (P50), and 13.5 years at P90. For Alternative 3, the illustrative capital cost ranges from $2.5B at P10 to $3.0B at median (P50) and $3.7B at P90, with an opening schedule ranging from 9.3 years at P10 to 10.6 years at median (P50) and 11.9 years at P90.

## Funding Strategy

The capital strategy identifies potential matches across federal grant and financing mechanisms. Scoping for all alternatives aligns with the FRA Corridor Identification and Development Program (Corridor ID), which provides $500K in planning assistance. The primary capital construction mechanism is the FRA Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (National), offering up to an 80.0% federal share ($1.6B) of median (P50) costs for Alternative 1, up to an 80.0% federal share ($2.4B) for Alternative 3, and a 79.1% federal share ($3.0B) for Alternative 2. Because the median (P50) cost of Alternative 2 exceeds the largest typical award of $3.0B, delivery would require phasing across multiple awards.

Additional federal support may include FRA Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) grants, which top out near $250M per award for discrete safety or capacity packages, representing 12.8% of median (P50) for Alternative 1, 6.6% for Alternative 2, and 8.2% for Alternative 3. Small-scale station investments may pursue USDOT BUILD grants, capped near $25M per award (representing 1.3% of median for Alternative 1, 0.7% for Alternative 2, and 0.8% for Alternative 3). Non-federal matching requirements could leverage USDOT Build America Bureau Railroad Rehabilitation and Improvement Financing (RRIF) loans, potentially financing 20% of median (P50) costs: $391M for Alternative 1, $758M for Alternative 2, or $608M for Alternative 3, contingent upon identified repayment sources.

## Risks

Project implementation faces several technical, institutional, and environmental considerations:

* Host railroad negotiations: A high share of alignment on existing rail rights-of-way does not grant operating permission, spare capacity, or track access agreements.
* Environmental and infrastructure hurdles: Alignments intersect waterway features (1 river crossings in Alternative 1 and Alternative 2; 2 river crossings in Alternative 3) and environmental areas (up to 8 environmental flag entries in Alternative 1 and 2 miles of new track in flagged areas in Alternative 2 and Alternative 3).
* Unmodeled operational parameters: No analysis was conducted for service frequency, timetable, and span of service; door-to-door or in-train travel time and competitiveness with driving, bus, or air; ridership or station-pair demand forecasts; on-time performance and reliability; operating and maintenance costs, fare revenue, and annual operating subsidy; track capacity, freight conflicts, train paths, and access agreements with host railroads; rolling stock, maintenance facilities, and electrification costs; or benefit-cost ratio, emissions, and safety outcomes.

## Next Steps

To advance the corridor development process, planning entities should pursue the following actions:

* Submit an application to FRA for the Corridor Identification and Development Program to secure $500K in Step 1 scoping support.
* Initiate preliminary discussions with freight host railroads regarding right-of-way access, dispatching feasibility, and shared track capacity.
* Conduct ridership modeling and travel-time competitiveness assessments against highway and intercity bus modes.
* Scope detailed operations and maintenance cost models, operating subsidy expectations, and rolling stock strategies.
* Refine conceptual alignments into engineered track designs to delineate environmental flag entries and river crossings.
